opus-5.5.text:
I think the paper does something valuable: it moves the conversation away from vague, sweeping statements about "AI risk" toward a more concrete framing. It tries to say which models deserve extra scrutiny, and that kind of specificity is what policymakers need.

Where I have real reservations is the reliance on compute as the main proxy for risk. Compute thresholds are attractive because they're measurable. You can count FLOPs, and it feels objective. But the relationship between training compute and capability, let alone compute and risk, is much less stable than people assume. We've seen over and over that smaller models, through better data, better optimization, distillation, or inference-time techniques, can match or beat much larger models from a year or two earlier. So a fixed threshold either becomes obsolete quickly or ends up capturing the wrong things.

There's also a deeper issue. Much of the risk in these systems isn't a property of the pre-trained artifact alone. It comes from how a model is deployed, what tools it's connected to, how it's fine-tuned, and who's using it. A framework centered on the frontier, meaning the biggest training runs, can give a false sense of security about everything below the line.

So I'd say it's a reasonable starting point, but it shouldn't be the foundation. If we build policy on it, it needs to be adaptive and revisited frequently. It should be paired with evaluations of actual capabilities and of deployment context, rather than treating a single number as a stand-in for danger. And we should be honest that the science of measuring risk is still very immature. Good policy should acknowledge that uncertainty rather than paper over it with a threshold that looks precise but isn't.

r001.rationale: The response critiques compute thresholds but does not identify a gap in specifying how to recognize when an LLM becomes a frontier model.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether a model can lose frontier-model status.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether proficiency in one risky skill is enough to classify a general-purpose model as frontier.

r004.rationale: It does not mention biosecurity evaluations or incentives to suppress recommendations.

r005.rationale: It discusses deployment context and model techniques, but does not observe that addressing one aspect of a general-purpose model can come at the expense of another.

r006.rationale: It says risk measurement is immature and compute thresholds can mislead, but does not connect that limitation to measuring a transition to frontier AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the Frontier Model paper is actually a really important contribution, and I want to give credit where it's due. It takes a really hard problem, which is how do you regulate a technology where the capabilities are emergent and hard to predict in advance, and it tries to put structure around it. The three-part framework, standard setting, registration and reporting, and compliance mechanisms, that's a sensible scaffolding, and it's one that policymakers can actually work with.

Where I have some hesitation is around the definition of what counts as a "frontier model" in the first place. The paper leans quite heavily on the idea that you can identify these models by proxies like compute thresholds, and I understand why. Compute is measurable, it's auditable, it's one of the few things you can actually observe from the outside. But in my own work I've seen how poorly compute tracks capability. We've watched smaller models trained on better data, or with better architectures, or with distillation from larger models, close the gap with models that were trained with ten or a hundred times the compute. So if you anchor the regulatory trigger to FLOPs, you're essentially regulating a snapshot of how models were built in 2023, and that snapshot is going to age very quickly.

The other thing I'd push on is the concept of "dangerous capabilities" as something that emerges unexpectedly. The paper frames this as a core motivation, that you can't know ahead of time what a model will be able to do. And there's truth to that. But I think it can also become a bit of a get-out-of-jail-free card. If we accept that capabilities are fundamentally unpredictable, then we're implicitly saying evaluation isn't really possible, and I don't think that's right. A lot of what gets called emergence is really an artifact of how we measure things, with discontinuous metrics, or evaluations that don't look at the right granularity. If you look at smoother measures, the trends are often far more predictable than people assume. So I'd want a policy framework that invests heavily in building out the science of evaluation, rather than one that treats unpredictability as a given.

And then the last point, which I think matters a lot for who actually bears the burden of this, is the question of concentration. If the regulatory trigger is a compute threshold, the entities that cross it are a handful of very well-resourced labs. On one level that's efficient, you're regulating a small number of actors. But it also means that the people setting the standards and the people being regulated are largely the same group, and that's a dynamic we should be clear-eyed about. I'd like to see much more emphasis on independent access for researchers, on open evaluation infrastructure, on making sure that the broader scientific community, and frankly the rest of the world outside of a few companies in a few countries, has a real seat at the table in defining what safe looks like.

So, to summarize: good framework as a starting point, I genuinely think it moved the conversation forward. But the devil is really in how you define the frontier, and I'd be cautious about building policy on compute as the primary lever, because I think the ground is shifting under that assumption faster than most people appreciate.

r001.rationale: The response critiques compute thresholds as an inadequate frontier-model proxy, but does not identify a failure to specify when an LLM becomes a frontier model as an implementation gap.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether a model can lose frontier-model status.

r003.rationale: The response does not address whether one risky skill is enough to classify a general-purpose model as frontier.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention biosecurity evaluations or incentives to suppress recommendations.

r005.rationale: The response does not observe that improving or addressing one aspect of a general-purpose model can come at another aspect’s expense.

r006.rationale: The response argues that some apparent unpredictability reflects measurement choices and calls for better evaluation science; it does not challenge measuring a transition to frontier AI because current model risk cannot be measured adequately.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful starting point, but I’m cautious about making the scale of a model the foundation for policy. The appeal is clear: compute is more measurable than something like capability or risk. But being measurable doesn’t necessarily make it the right proxy.

A model’s potential for harm depends on what it can do, who has access to it, and how it’s deployed. A smaller model used in a consequential setting can warrant substantial scrutiny, while a larger model may pose very different risks depending on the safeguards around it. And as algorithms become more efficient, a fixed compute threshold may miss capabilities that previously required much more compute.

So I’d treat the framework as one input into policy, alongside evaluations of specific capabilities and the context of use. The question I’d want us to keep asking is: does this rule actually capture the harm we’re trying to prevent?

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: is it a useful framework for thinking about risk, and is it a sufficient basis for policy? Those are different standards. Without knowing which paper you mean, I’d be cautious about assessing its specific proposals.

But for a frontier-model framework, the central question is what makes a model worthy of additional scrutiny. If we use training compute or model size as a proxy for risk, that may be administratively convenient, but it doesn’t directly tell us what a system can do or how it will be used. Capabilities can change with more efficient algorithms, and the deployment context matters enormously.

So I’d want a framework that connects requirements to demonstrated capabilities and evidence of harm, and that can adapt as the technology changes. I’d also ask who can afford to comply. We should be careful that the cost of oversight doesn’t end up concentrating development in the hands of a few companies.
